utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Could we have appearances for this afternoon, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Dan Saxon, Barney Thomas, and Ms. Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Saxon. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Chad Mair, Tina Drolec, Novak Lukic and, Greg Guy-Smith on behalf of Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Just before we carry on to say that the Chamber is sitting this afternoon pursuant to rule 15 bis because -- in the absence of Judge David who is not in town. He is out of town. Yes, Mr. Saxon, you wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes. I was going to call the next witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, can we do a little bit of housekeeping matters. First of all, just to say that it may be that a message was sent to the parties, but just to make it abundantly clear, there is a Plenary this afternoon at 5.00. Members of the Chamber are expected to attend. So hopefully it will be a very short Plenary, just one item on the agenda. That's that. Secondly, there is an oral decision that the Chamber would like to render in relation to some of the motions that have been coming through quite recently, and which I think -- about which I think a decision should be rendered before we call the next witness. This is going to be an oral decision. The Trial Chamber is seized of a Prosecution motion for leave to file a 10th supplemental Rule 65 ter list and a request to tender certain exhibits from the bar table filed on the 16th of October, 2009, hereinafter referred to separately as Prosecution 65 ter list motion and third bar table motion. On the 23rd of October, 2009, the Defence filed a response to the Prosecution's 65 ter list motion only with respect to the expert report and associated documents therewith. In light of the arguments submitted by the Prosecution, the Trial Chamber, pursuant to Rule 54 and 65 ter of the rules, finds the amendment of the Prosecution ter list in to the expert report of Major-General Melvin and the associated documents to be in the interests of justice. The Trial Chamber remains seized of the Prosecution's 65 ter list motion with respect to the remaining documents. The Trial Chamber is also seized of a motion for extension of time to response to both Prosecution second bar table motion and Prosecution motion for leave to file a 10th supplemental Rule 65 ter list and request to tender certain exhibits from the bar table filed confidentially on the 22nd of October, 2009. The Prosecution filed its response to this motion today requesting that the Trial Chamber should deny the Defence motion for extension of time or alternatively that the Defence be ordered to respond to the Prosecution 65 ter list motion within 48 hours of a decision by the Trial Chamber on this matter. The Trial Chamber notes in this regard that pursuant to rules 126 bis of the rules, the Defence has time to file its response to the Prosecution 65 ter list motion until the 30th of October, 2009. The Trial Chamber has considered the arguments advanced by the Defence, in particular related to the complexity of bar table motions and the circumstances in which the motions were filed and has decided as follows: To grant in part the motion of the Defence for extension of time pursuant to rule 127 of the rules. Accordingly, the Trial Chamber authorises the Defence to file its response to both the Prosecution's second and third bar table motions by the 5th of November, 2009. Two, to deny the Prosecution request to expedite the Defence response to the Prosecution 65 ter list motion. Mr. Saxon. You may call your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. At this time, then, the Prosecution calls Major-General Mungo Melvin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Major-General. Will you please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated. Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. Will you state your full name for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: My name is Major-General Robert Adam Mungo Simpson Melvin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. And today I will address you as General Melvin; is that all right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: That is fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well. And General Melvin, are you currently a -- actually, before I begin, I see you've brought in a small binder and it's on the desk in front of you. Just so that it's clear to the Chamber and to the Defence, it's my understanding that that binder contains a copy of your expert report for these proceedings and the source materials that you refer to in the footnotes. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: That is correct. It is solely my report, together with the source material for the footnotes that I put in my note -- in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just so we are clear, is it my understanding there are no other notes contained within the documentation in front of the gentleman?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And you heard the question of my colleague, so then your binder contains no other notes?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: That is correct. The only exception to that is I've made one or two -- underlined a couple of parts of my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Perhaps for everybody's comfort, may we give the Defence half a second to just glance at the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I note that in the report, the final version of the report of General Melvin consisting of some 24 pages, there are a number of interlineation and handwritten notes contained in his report distinct from the issue of footnotes. There are some names and some other matters that are contained in his report that are not in the report that I have. I'm wondering if at some point it would be convenient just for me to get a copy of the actual document that the General is using during his testimony. I think that probably will settle or resolve any concerns that I might have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That would be perfectly fine with the Prosecution. We can do it at the first break.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. If we can please show General Melvin and the persons present what is 65 ter 9571, please, it's the curriculum vitae of General Melvin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: While we are waiting for that, General Melvin, I'm not going to take you completely through your CV, but can you just tell us about your military education?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: My military education started formally with attendance at the Royal Military Academy at Sandhurst between 1974 and 1975. It was then followed by various courses, the most significant of which was attendance at the German Armed Forces Commanded Staff College at Hamburg between 1986 and 1988. I then attending the British Armed Forces Higher Command and Staff course in 1998, and that completes my military education.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, in the second paragraph of your CV you list a number of positions and operational service and in command during your career, so I'm not going to ask you to repeat that. Approximately how many years have you served in the army of the United Kingdom?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Since entering the British army in the summer of 1974, I have served 35 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And your present position?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Currently I'm held strength of the Chief of General Staff of the British army. I am in fact between two formal appointments. My last formal appointment was as the general officer commanding the United Kingdom support command in Germany, and I'm going to move next month to be the senior army member at the Royal College of Defence studies in London.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Melvin, have you written any publications related to military affairs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Several. The most prominent of which I was the principal author of the "British Army Doctrine Publication Volume 2 Command," which I wrote in 1994 and was published in 1995. Ten years later, I was the editor and co-author of a successor publication, "Army Doctrine Publication Land Operations," which was written in 2004 and published in 2005. In addition to that, I've contributed widely to joint and multinational doctrine works and have written on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And since the publication of your work on command in 1995, have you returned to that subject?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Indeed. I wrote the chapter on command in "Army Doctrine Publication Land Operations," Chapter 6, which I've quoted in my report. That is a condensed version and revised version of what I wrote ten years previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Is command considered -- the subject of command per se, is that considered to be an academic specialisation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Not at all. Command, first and foremost, is a practical matter which is exercised on a daily basis across all military forces. I have been privileged to research the matter and have written about it. And my writings are based on both personal practical experience and that which I've researched and observed on others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mentioned a publication called "Land Ops Doctrine," which was published in 2005. Are you doing any additional work on that publication?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Yes. Further to submitting my CV, I've been asked to mentor the next edition which is due to be written in 2010. I will be looking at all aspects of that publication. I will assist it. I will not be directly responsible, however, at this stage for writing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Have you taught any courses related to military affairs?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Yes, several. I was a member of the directing or teaching staff at the British Army Staff College in 1993 and 1994. I was subsequently a member of the directing staff and the deputy director of our higher command and staff course at the Joint Services Command and Staff College between 1998 and 2000. And subsequent to that, I've been a guest lecturer at that college and other institutions on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this point I would ask that the Chamber admit this curriculum vitae, 65 ter 9571.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Just before we do that, I notice that in Prosecution confidential submission of expert report of Major-General Mungo Melvin dated the 12th of October, 2009, the Prosecution says that in August 2010 Major-General Melvin left the position of General office of commanding the United Kingdom support command. And I just -- is there something that needs to be corrected there?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The correction, that was a typographical error by myself, Your Honour, for which I apologise. It should say 2009.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. 65 ter 9571 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This becomes Exhibit P2771. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to direct your attention, General Melvin, to your report itself, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And can we please call up what is now 65 ter 9572.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, General -- we'll wait for the B/C/S version to come up. General, at paragraphs 1.1 through 1.6 of your report, you describe your task and the four questions that you were asked to respond to. At paragraph 1.2, which is on the very first page, you describe how General Dannatt had asked you to take on the task of preparing an expert report for this case. And you say: "I had already read into the case to some extent." Are you following me?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you be more specific about what you had read at that point?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: I had read, at that stage, two documents. One was the -- your set, Mr. Saxon's -- the original six questions which you had sent to General Dannatt's office. And secondly, before I looked at those in order to give me some context, I had looked on the internet and had read the indictment against -- against General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And at that time did you see a document titled "Command and Control"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: But I did not spend -- I did spend enough -- I did not have enough time to read it in full. I glanced at the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At paragraph 1.4 --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And this is on page 3 of the English version and also the same page of the B/C/S version, it begins there in the English version and then continues on to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: On page 3 of the English version, the last sentence of that paragraph 1.4 refers to the Ministry of Defence's Trials and Inquiries Unit, TIU. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Is that reference correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: No. And on my original I've deleted the word "trials" and inserted "Tribunals." That was a typographical error of mine which I'd failed to spot prior to the final submission of the report dated the 17th of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we could move down just to the next paragraph, paragraph 1.5, in the very first line of paragraph 1.5, you say: "I can confirm that I received some input on factual [measures] from others." Can you explain what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Yes, indeed - and I'm referring here to my notes here - I received advice from two members of the Ministry of Defence United Kingdom legal services, Mr. Stewart Howard and a Mr. Humphrey Morrison who gave me some advice on legal phraseology. They gave me no advice on the doctrinal input to my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well. At paragraph 1.6, we see the four questions that you were asked to consider, and I'm not going to ask you to read them now because we are going to look at each one of those questions as we go through your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could turn to paragraph 2.1, please, which is on page 4 of the English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about the methodology that you used to answer these four questions. And there -- at paragraph 2.4 it has a subtitle called "Background." And can you just briefly summarise what you are trying to convey in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Yes, may I take your first question about methodology first and then I'll return to background, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you prefer.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: The methodology which I've described if my report from pages 4 onwards is an attempt to give an explanation to the approach that I took in writing the report. It parallels an approach I would take for writing the majority of the military reports that I have to do. It -- in the starting point is an explanation of the approach that you are taking and to provide some context and background as necessary. So I've done that in two ways: I've provided general context, particularly in terms of terminology and doctrine before I answer the four questions; and then, using similar approach, I've tried to provide some background or context to each of the four answers I've given to the four questions. That, I think, I hope answers the first part of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Moving on to the rationale --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, no, General. I'm really only interested for now in paragraph 2.1, thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I think you've dealt with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn to paragraph 2.4, which is on page 8 of the English version and page 8 of the B/C/S version. Paragraph 2.4 has the subtitle "Approach of This Report" can you explain to the Judges please, General, what was the general approach that you took in the writing of your report.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Well, my approach was, bearing in mind that I was asked four questions which are largely of a doctrinal nature, was to provide a general document which provided an explanation of command, gave some examples of definitions, and then gave some specific answers to the questions that you had posed. I wanted to stress in the approach of my report that I wasn't going to go into any specific matters pertinent to the case or the indictment of General Perisic. I didn't think I was qualified to do so, and, in any case, I did not have time to research that. So I wanted to make that a very clear constraint or, as you were, limitation to my report very clear to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I notice, Major-General, that you do say in that paragraph that you consider the general context of command rather than the specific, and then the next sentence you go to say that in so doing, you provide some background doctrinal material on command drawn from the United Kingdom and the NATO forces. Can you reconcile those two views? It looks to me like you first say you are giving your general doctrinal context and then you move on specifically to the UK and NATO without giving us a general context of command. But it looks like you are being specific to NATO and British forces.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise if the wording wasn't sufficiently clear. Let me try and elaborate to answer your question. The -- when I was referring to the general context of command, I was referring to a general doctrinal context of command rather than a specific circumstances of command pertaining to any commander at a particular place or time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And I, from my own experience, my quoting of UK national and NATO done doctrine with which I'm familiar, I used that to mean the general context of command. May I -- Your Honour, I see I've not clarified it for you. My --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, I understand what you say, and I just failed to understand how UK command as understood in -- how command as understood in the UK or in the NATO forces can be seen as a general context of command.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I perhaps have -- I have by over-familiarity and bearing in mind that my service of 35 years has been within the -- with a very minor exception has been entirely within the British and NATO command, I have taken it with respect largely as read as that as a general context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, that's the universal knowledge for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From my experience.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: From your experience. But it is not the universal context of command. Because an Afghanistan force, a Mozambique [Realtime transcript read in error "Muslim"] force somewhere might have other commands which you are not familiar with.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can -- one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: While you are asking for a moment, the "Muslim" after Afghanistan force that appears on the transcript should read "Mozambique" force.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Following up on His Honour Judge Moloto's questions to you a moment ago, you -- in paragraph 2.4 when you refer to the general context of command -- I'm going to leave this for now. I may come back to this. Are you aware of any modern armies, General Melvin, in which what you describe as the general context of command would not apply based on your knowledge and experience?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: If I may refer back to what I wrote in my report at paragraph 2.3.1, I think that would be important to stress what I meant, bearing in mind the discussion with His Honour on the subject, what I mean by "general context." For a specific army coalition or alliance there is a -- or a commanders within such a force, there is a general context. I've suggested here in my report that it is based on a foundation of education and training. That's what I mean here by the general context. And I've also set out that I believe it to be uniformly the case that in modern armies, modern forces, that that context command will be set up formally in laws, regulations, administrative instructions, and doctrine publications, and notes. I've also said in my report at the top of page 7, that that general context is also passed on informally through established custom and practice. My experience of modern armies has been, as I've tried to clarify to the Court, primarily of the British army and of fellow NATO forces. I have some other experience of other forces, but that's much more limited. But I believe, in answering your question, what I've said is the basic issue of the general context.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Does that mean your answer -- well, let me go back to my original question then. Are you aware of any modern armies in which what you describe as the general context of command would not apply based on your knowledge and experience?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Based on my knowledge and experience, I'm not aware of any modern armies where this generally written context would not apply, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn, please, to paragraph 2.5 of General Melvin's report, which -- this is on page 8, I believe, in both versions. Bottom of page 8 in the English version. There it is in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Paragraph 2.5, General, is subtitled, "Detailed Method." Can you explain, please, what was the detailed method that you used in responding to these four questions?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: As I've outlined earlier, my approach in answering any question is to examine the context first; and therefore, in attempting to answer each of the four questions posed, I have first undertaken a general examination of the question trying to gain an understanding of what is meant by the question, what may lay behind that question, in simple terms an analysis of the question. I then set out specific answers to the questions and, as stated in my report, where the question consisted a number of sub-questions, I've addressed those sequentially in the order presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let's turn our minds now to question 1, which is at -- starts at paragraph 3.1, page 9 of the English version and of the B/C/S version. The very first part of that question says the following: "Describe the generally accepted principles governing cooperation between the military forces of two countries." Now, in paragraphs 3.1.1 through 3.1.10, you describe these principles. I'd like to take you, please, to paragraph 3.1.11, which is on page 12 of the English and B/C/S versions. And there we see the next portion of question 1 which says: "Describe the concepts of command and control, operational control, tactical control, et cetera, as they apply in this context." Can you please explain to us briefly what the concept of command means, the concept of control means?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Well, I -- in order to help you and the Court, I would request respectfully that we return to an earlier part of the report and to page 5 of my report and subparagraph 2.21, where I describe the terms "command" and "control." That's paragraph 2.21.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Are these terms distinct are or are they synonymous?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: They are often informally intermixed, but they are not, as I stress here, not synonymous. I have quoted here, directly from the NATO doctrine, command and control terms which are differentiated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And command, very briefly?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: A command, as doctrinally set out here, is the more inclusive of the two terms, it is the authority vested individual to direct, coordinate, or control armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Whilst control is more of a process through which a commander, assisted by his staff, actually organises or directs or coordinates those activities which he has directed. So in clarifying the difference between command and control, as I make clear in the next paragraph, control, by my understanding, by my writing, and by my teaching, control is a subset of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: All right. If we can turn back, please, to page 12 in the English and B/C/S version. And we'll take a look at paragraph 3.1.13.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And in that paragraph, General, you refer in the very first line to a concept called "command states." Can you explain that concept, please?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: The term "command state" is a military term used widely across NATO. I cannot confirm whether or not it's used in other armies. I suspect it is. And what it does is define formally the command relationship between superior commanders and subordinate commanders, between formations and subordinate formations. Those command states are carefully defined in the NATO glossary, and I've set those terms out on pages 13 and 14 of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: One of those command states that you described is full command. Can you describe what that is, please?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: I quote that the full command is: "The military authority and responsibility of a commander to issue orders to subordinates. It covers every aspect of military operations and administration, and exists only within national services."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could turn to page 13, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I believe still on the bottom of page 12 we saw full command. We see at the top of page 13 in English the concept of full command. Then we see --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we could turn to the next page in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You refer to a command state called "operational command." Can you explain what that means?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: When we move out of the national realm into the multinational realm certainly within NATO and in coalition operations involving NATO forces, the most frequent command states used are those of operational command and operational control. Taking the operational command first, to answer your question, is, I quote: "The authority granted to a commander to assign missions or tasks to subordinate commanders, to deploy units to reassign forces, and to retain or delegate operational and/or tactical control as the commander deems necessary." And I further quote, and this is the important distinction between operational command and full command: "It doesn't include responsibility normally for administration or discipline."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And operational control, can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Operational control is a lesser command state than operational command. Again, I quote: "An authority delegated to a commander to direct forces assigned so that a commander may accomplish specific missions or tasks which are usually limited by function, time, or location." I would stress, however, that the power to a commander given in operational control is significantly less than that he would otherwise have under operational command. And quoting again from the NATO doctrine in my report, under operational control: "It does not include authority to assign the separate employment of components of the units concerned."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would operational control then include the authority and responsibility to discipline or not?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Not -- not normally. The disciplinary chain is normally retained through a full command or national command chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So if we just look -- if we are looking at page 13 of the English version where we see full command, operational command, and operational control, which command state would be the broadest and which would be the most restrictive on this page?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: The broadest one is, without doubt, full command. And the most limited of the three is operational control.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just ask, is it possible to envisage or have you come across a situation where two competent parts of full command, namely military operations and administration, vest in two separate organs of command and not in one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as I understand it, no, because the administrative, as I said, and full command chains are normally the one. But to clarify, there can be - this is why we have to couch the term "normally" in doctrine - there can be situations by which, under multinational arrangements, some aspects of administration or logistics could be provided on a multinational basis. For example, water, fuel, could be provided on a multinational basis, not on a national basis. But that's unlikely to pertain when we get to discipline. In my experience, discipline is retained by the national command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On that point, in your knowledge of command, have you come across the concept of resubordination? And if so, how is command exercised in the situation where there's been a resubordination of some units to some other command other than the national command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you referring to, Your Honour, to subordination, I'm not aware of the term you are specifically using here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The term "resubordination," you are not aware of that term?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you are not aware of the term, then there's no point asking the question. I will drop the question. Thank you. You may proceed. Before you proceed, sorry, Mr. Saxon. You have indicated, Major-General, examples of administration as relating to provision of fuel and water. My actual question was, well, I was envisaging under the heading of administration, payment of salaries, promotions of officers, pensioning of officers, that kind of administration. Are you aware of that kind of administration --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- being vested in a separate organ of command from the organ which bears operational command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you for clarifying that for me. It terms of administration -- personnel administration, there can be cases where another force will undertake some administrative functions on behalf of another one. But I -- but as I set out later in my report, when it comes to things like pay and pensions and discipline, those are normally retained by the national command authority, i.e., that authority that sends either forces or individuals to join another command either on a multinational basis or on another nation's basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How does the national office or the national command exercise discipline if it is not operationally close to the theatre of war to observe any misdemeanors or any crimes committed by the forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is simply answered, Your Honour, that in almost all cases there will be appointed, whatever the nation concerned, a national contingent commander who will be appointed for that specific circumstance to deal with discipline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. You deal with the national contingent commander later in your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In a situation where there's no such office, how does that get implemented?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if for the example that there were no formally appointed national contingent commander, it would be incumbent on the senior national officer in pursuance of his normal duties to maintain good order and discipline of his unit, of the soldiers, sailors, or airmen under his command. Those of his own nation. So he would have first and foremost that responsibility to ensure good order and military discipline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. As I understand you, Major-General, within this unit that is operating in a multinational situation, there would be a commander, whether he is an NCC or some other commander, but the most senior commander from the contributing nation who is directly responsible for the maintenance of discipline within the unit under him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Melvin, following up on Judge Moloto's last question, suppose there is no in-theatre - if I can use that term - national commander appointed to oversee matters of discipline, what responsibility, if any, would the national military commander or commanders back in the sending nation have if they are aware that their troops that are part of a multinational force or serving with another nation have engaged in criminal conduct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: As I think I make clear in my report, there is always a duty to act in the event of criminal actions or activity being detected. As I've stated to His Honour the Judge, that even if a national contingent commander is not appointed, it would fall on the senior ranking national officer to report any incidents along the lines you've suggested and to take appropriate steps at the very least to launch some form of investigation and to report that immediately up his command chain to the sending or contributing force. Back in the nation, or back in the home country, there would be likewise a responsibility to take action on that report or on information being received by other sources. And in my experience where this has happened, then there has been investigations launched within the theatre of operations and, if necessary, an investigative team may also be sent out by the contributing nation to investigate that in the theatre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And would that responsibility to take action that you've described back in the home country, would that apply even when the troops that were sent to the receiving nation were serving under the operational control of that a receiving nation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Very much so because as the command states -- a differentiation between the command states are made clear, even if that national force was operating under the operational control of a different national commander in a multinational context, the disciplinary chain will remain primarily a national one and therefore there is a responsibility to act both in theatre and as necessary to act from the sending state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Back to my question. That would depend, of course, on reports being given to the contributing state of commissions of crime by the contributed members of the force on the theatre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, primarily. But I don't think - and no specific example springs to mind - I don't think we can exclude the possibility of the sending state reacting purposefully and appropriately if it were to receive information from another source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's true. But all I'm saying is in the normal course of events, as I understand, and you correct me here because you are the specialist on command and control, I would imagine that command and control has as its inherent -- as a systemic composition of it a line of communication from the theatre up the chain of command to the national commander and back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. The whole system would depend on timely reports and returns on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's correct. And, therefore, it is through this reporting mechanism that the national commander gets to know of any commission of crimes that takes place on the theatre of war which then triggers his duty to do something?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that is by far the most important and the most reliable source. I, in my earlier response, was indicating I couldn't exclude a responsive and responsible national command authority from taking action.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On hearing it from another source.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On hearing it from another source. That is all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hear that. That's why -- okay. Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time, would you like to take the first break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: At half past.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Half past, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Melvin, is the distinction between the two terms "command" and "control" always the same for all armies?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: I think in the practical usage, as I've tried to indicate in my report, there can be some difference because informally the terms command and control in certainly my 35 years' experience can often be interchanged. But it doctrinally and in specific circumstance of the command states they are not interchanged. The emphasis between command and control does change. What is not helpful is the expression common in all armies and all armed forces, command and control. I have waged a lone fight to remove this term unsuccessfully because, as I've argued and have written and has been largely accepted, but not fully, that command is an element -- I correct myself, control is an element of command and not the other way about. So there is some -- to answer your question, across armies, there is some difference of emphasis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What about in the context of particular command states such as full command, operational command, operational control, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Here I make an important distinction whereas the terms command and control are loosely used in general military conversation, publications, when we get down to the specific issues of command states, the terms command and control, particularly when they are applied in the specific terminology, full command, operational command, operational control, tactical command, or tactical control, are very precisely used.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And why is that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Coming back to the multinational context, the command states are a very specific and very particular way in which the freedom of multinational commanders are limited by the troop contributing nations. And I give a specific example, I think, in my report. The distinct between, for example, operational command and operational control is significant. The operational control command state is more limiting and it specifically does not include the authority to split up component units. Why would a national commander be concerned about that? Well, it could be, and this is often the evidence given to have a restrictive command state, that though tactically the national commander might be well within his rights to request the break-up of a specific formation, the national command authority might not be able to provide the appropriate logistic support for it. So these command states represent a set of check and balances within a multinational framework.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well. General, focusing again on page 13, and there's a box on page 13 with the subtitle "Important Note." I want you to turn your mind to that for a moment. How is the term "command" used in an international context, or in the context of a multinational military force?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Well, so you've referred the Court and me to the boxed important note on page 13?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: May I first of all stress, that is a direct quote from the NATO glossary. And what that note is trying to do is to make it clear that within the multinational context internationally, the term "command" does not imply full command. It is going to imply a command of a lesser state either operational command or operational control or tactical command or tactical control. In the NATO or coalition context, no multinational commander would exercise full command, so therefore when a multinational commander gives an order by virtue of his appointment when he commands subordinate commanders and their formations, he cannot exercise full command because he doesn't have it. That is retained by the troop contributing the national command chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn, please, to the next page in English and B/C/S. This will be paragraph 3.1.16.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And it has the subtitle "Role of the Sending Country (or State)." What is the role of a sending country or state which contributes forces to a multinational military operation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: The sending state, as you would imagine, it would be responsible for preparing -- preparing the force and training it. That's one of its responsibilities. As an issue, I did not go into it in my report. But what the troop contributing nation, as I state in my report, retains the responsibility to administer the individuals concerned and as previously discussed in court, pay promotion and retirement issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Would disciplinary powers also be retained?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Disciplinary powers are usually retained within the national command chain. Ultimate authority remaining with the national command chain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn, please, to page 15 in the English and B/C/S versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We'll take a look at question 2, General Melvin. Question 2 says: "Describe any historical context that you are aware of in which a military has seconded personnel to the operational control of the military of another country while continuing to provide all remuneration including enhanced pay and pension rights for combat service in that other country, as well as retain its right to make final determination on the promotion and retirement of those officers, and does not exercise its ability to discipline those soldiers for breaches of military or international law."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we go to the next page, please, in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, General Melvin, there we see paragraph 3.2.3 that in order to answer the question you created this table. Can you explain -- can you please explain why you created this table and what you intend to demonstrate by it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Well, first of all, in -- it's a response to answering your question 2 which was set a number of conditions. This table is my own formulation, because in my experience and my knowledge of both national and multinational doctrine, I hadn't seen a question formulated in this manner before. And, therefore, I attempted to answer the question from first principles and took each of the three conditions which were contained in the question and analysed them to expose what I believe to be a general application, but also, where appropriate, I observed any exceptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: So if we look, General, at the upper left-hand corner, the left-hand column "Condition." And the first condition is where the sending state continues to provide all remuneration including enhanced pay and pension rights for combat service in that other country, what then, according to -- would be, according to your knowledge, would be the general application?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Well, as I state in the table, the sending state under its full command responsibilities is normally -- remains responsible for that administration, pay, and pensions, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Might there be an exception to that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: The exception could be that the sending state might elect to pay the individual or top up that individual's pay. That could be done either directly to the individual, or more likely, it would be indirectly in, i.e., from a government-to-government basis under a bilateral agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But on this box you are not talking the bilateral government-to-government agreement. You are talking of actually some kind of securing their release from the sending state as if this is a luring of the soldiers. This is what I wanted to understand from you. What do you mean by securing release from the sending state. Are you, by that, suggesting that they would then, sort of, desert their national state army --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- and then join -- what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at all, Your Honour. What I'm meaning here is that the sending state might wish to have some recompense for sending its forces or individuals to another nation, and in addition to that, that the receiving nation might wish to make it attractive to the sending state or the individuals of the sending state. I'll give you an example, that the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But wait a minute. The box clearly says: "The receiving state may elect to pay seconded individuals" - not to pay the sending state, seconded individuals - "in order to attract suitably qualified personnel or to secure their release from the sending state." It almost suggested to me, and I want you to clear my mind if I misread you, it almost suggested a clandestine move on the part of the receiving state to attract soldiers of the sending state onto its side. I'll pay you better than your state is paying you. Is that what should be read into that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, with respect, Your Honour, you may be reading a little bit too much into what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But if I may, just to clarify the point, I made two qualifying remarks to what I said in the box. I made the point the paid seconded individuals, that doesn't need to be directly paying the individuals, that could be through the sending -- the sending state. If I were, I could expand that box to make that point further clear. I'm just trying to condense what I wrote there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Can I be just clear, what you are saying here, is this covered by the caveat you make at the bottom of page 15?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I made a specific caveat here because my reading this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are just giving your opinions here. This is not professional opinion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it is a professional opinion, but it's not based on a large amount of documentary evidence. There's no doctrinal foundation for what I'm saying. That's why I put the caveat, a very clear caveat there, Your Honour. Because the question as posed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you said, therefore, I've offered -- including, I've offered only opinions here based on my personal knowledge and experience.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you have source documents to substantiate what you mention in these blocks here on page 16?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that's my point. There's no -- I have found no doctrinal foundation for these observations. I've only produced this table to my best knowledge and experience to assist answering the questions as put to me by Mr. Saxon to help the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Before we break, General, just so that the record is clear, when I asked you, and, Your Honours, I believe this is on page 30, line 11 of the LiveNote which is now gone from my screen, when I asked you about the first exception in this table, you started off by answering the sending state may elect to pay, did you mean to say the receiving state?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: I have -- I have stated in the general application the sending state.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: And in exception, I've talked the receiving state.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well. And in the exception column where you use the phrase "or to secure their release from the sending state," did you mean to imply their permanent release?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me. I'll object to the leading at this point. He can explain to us what he meant to imply as opposed to you suggesting to him what he means to imply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would uphold that, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well then I've got to rephrase my question then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do so, and let's take a break after he has answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: What did you mean by the phrase "secure their release"?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: I meant here, and it was implicit, I hope, that the release would be for a period of service. And hence I eluded to, in my exception, an example of loan service which occurs in the British army where individuals are detached from their service with the British army to serve in the armed forces of another nation such as the Sultan of Oman's armed forces for a specific period of time. I did not mean here any notion of a permanent release of the individual. This was for specific periods of duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Shall we take the first break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take the break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we can turn again to paragraph 3.2.3 of 65 ter 9572, page 16, there we have it, of General Melvin's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And we were reviewing this table, General, that you had created to answer question number 2. And the second condition I see in the middle row where the sending state retains its right to make final determinations on the promotion and retirement of those officers, and you say, in the next column, that the general application would remain as in the -- with respect to the first condition already discussed, but might there be an exception in that circumstance?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: I could only envisage very rare exceptions to that, hence I put in general application that I believe the issues which you raise in your second condition, determinations of promotion, retirement, those should be retained by the sending state. The reason for that is that they would normally take a career view of you on the overall perspective of an individual's career taking into the individual's past activities and future potential into account. And that could not be done by the receiving state.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm not sure if the transcript picked up the first start of your answer because I see at line 17 when I asked whether there might be an exception in that circumstance you said "I could only envisage it very ..." and there's a word missing.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Rarely. Rarely is the word I used, rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, before I forget, you and I are speaking in the same language, and that makes it -- that makes communication easier for the two of us but can make life very difficult for the interpreters. And they've requested that we try to pause between question and answer. If we could try to remember to do that. In the bottom row of the same column, 3.2.3, the same table, the condition where the sending state does not exercise its ability to discipline those soldiers for breaches of military or international law. And in your general application you say this happens very rarely. Why is that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: As I stated in my report, that is because the sending state usually retains full powers of discipline over its seconded personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Might there be an exception, however?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: The only exception that I could find in my research, but it was a very specific one so I didn't put it in the report, was a historical exception. And that was the case where British commonwealth forces were attached to British forces during the Second World War, and powers of discipline were passed from the sending state to the receiving state, in this case to Britain, for very practical reasons because it wasn't going be practical for the sending state, in this case perhaps Canada or Australia, to exercise the powers of discipline over individuals that were stationed in Britain, for example. That is the historical exception I found, but I could not find a contemporary one, therefore I did not include that in my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what would make impossible for a state like Australia or Canada, for instance, to maintain discipline over its forces who are in Britain? If they have an NCC, for instance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, nowadays and with modern communications, Your Honour, I don't think it would be very difficult at all. I think that's -- hence I very carefully made the point in answering my question this was an historical example where I think it was a pragmatic response but would not necessarily apply today. Today, you are absolutely right. There would be a national contingent commander and all but for the most, I imagine, trivial issues the -- as I've stated and as you've indicated, Your Honour, the nations would retain their disciplinary powers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what in modern days has happened that makes it easier to maintain -- to retain that control which was absent during World War II? Was it World War II or World War I?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was making the example of the Second World war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Second World War, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, the answer is a simple one. I think modern communications and both in passage of information and modern communications in terms of being able to move people around the world so much more quickly has made it much easier for the nations of contributing nations to exercise their disciplinary powers. So I think that is the simple reason for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think my specific question really relates to what in the modern communications is there which was not there in World War II which make it is easier to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, both electronic communications, phone, e-mail, but also physical communications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was phone not there in World War II?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The e-mail certainly wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The e-mail wasn't there, but the telegram and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Telegram and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- and phone were there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But it was not only a matter of communications, I'm also talking about physical communications. In the time of World War II, it was simply not as easy to move around the globe as it is today. And also, I would suggest, there were different historical conditions pertaining at the time. I can imagine that the -- during the Second World War, and again I made the specific example here, Canadian or Dominion forces or Australian forces, could be put under British command in a way that could not be envisioned today. Times have changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What role would a factor that the commonwealth forces would have looked up to Britain as the mother country play in that scenario as compared to states that are equal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, that's a very important distinction. Historically, I think you are absolutely right to observe that those dominion countries looked then to the United Kingdom as a mother country. In terms of states of equal rank or equal quality, then, I think, there would be that -- those conditions would not pertain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And in World War II there were allies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And did -- apart from the dominion countries, did any countries of equal state ever relinquish their right of discipline to any other state other than the dominions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is an area, Your Honour, I've not researched in any detail, but from my general military historical knowledge, I cannot recall such a case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm going to move on now. If we can take a look -- if we can scroll down on the bottom of the page in B/C/S, please. All right. If we could turn to the next page in B/C/S and on the same page in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Paragraph 3.2.4, General. The first sentence says: "Rephrased within an alliance or coalition context, it is normal for contributing nations not only to retain responsibility for pay, promotion, and retirement, but also for discipline of their seconded personnel under operational control." Might there been exceptions to this general rule? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: There could be exceptions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And to your knowledge and experience, are such exceptions common or rare?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: The only general range of exceptions is that which I cover in the following paragraph of 3.2.5 which relates to stationing of forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: 3.2.5 you refer to a major exception. Can you briefly discuss what that exception is or explain what it is.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: This is where I'm trying to explain an exception to the general rule I've described hitherto. Under a status of forces agreement, a NATO one with which I'm familiar, there is a split of jurisdiction between the sending and receiving states. As I state in my report, normally all internal military offences would be considered as those which should be retained in jurisdiction terms by the sending state. However, if the receiving state had a particular interest in a case, a serious criminal offence affecting a national of that receiving state would be a good example, in my experience it would be unlikely to waive jurisdiction in this case. I have personal experience of dealing with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But this is an exception that you are aware of that comes as a result of some agreement as you say in paragraph 3.2.5?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Without an agreement you are not aware of this because this is what I was asking you just before Mr. Saxon asked you the question, this is what I was asking you, apart from the dominions, you were not aware of any other such retention of disciplinary jurisdiction by the receiving state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I'm not Your Honour. That's why I made that exception clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's right. And in the absence of any agreement, you are not aware of anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And in this exception, you are saying the receiving state, if it has an interest maybe because of the involvement of its national would then want to retain jurisdiction, would that receiving state be retaining jurisdiction to try an officer of another state for a war crime, or only for compensation towards its officer, or for an ordinary criminal case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot give you, from my personal experience here, Your Honour, a substantive answer for the issue of war crime. But for a serious crime against a person, I can give a recent example within my competence and my last job as the general officer commanding of the United Kingdom support command. I had to deal with a case in which a British soldier was alleged to have raped a German national away from a military base and, therefore, the German legal system, in my view rightly, did not waive its jurisdiction, it retained jurisdiction. That individual appeared in front of a German court to answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And where had the rape allegedly taken place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Had taken place in a German town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: German territory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: German territory, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And that would have been an ordinary criminal case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was an ordinary, though a very severe, criminal case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Very severe. But ordinary criminal -- not a war crime.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, it was not a war crime, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Melvin, I'd like to ask you, please, to turn your mind to question number 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could go -- keep the same page in English but go forward one more page in the B/C/S version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Question 3 says: "Summarise the basic principles governing military discipline and how they apply in settings in which multinational forces are cooperating. What are the obligations of the commander of one of the contributing forces in the event he becomes aware that his personnel that have been placed under the operational control of another force are being engaged in criminal conduct by the foreign commander with operational control."

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can go forward one more page in English, please, remain in the same page in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, if you could turn your mind to paragraph 3.3.3, which is subtitled "The Nature of Disciplinary Responsibility." Can you summarise that paragraph for us, please?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Yes. As I've stated, discipline is an absolutely essential part and basis of the efficiency and effectiveness of a military force. Without discipline, a force cannot operate properly. And therefore, both the individuals within a force have the responsibility to act in a disciplined manner, and their commanders, at all levels, have a responsibility to ensure that discipline is maintained. And further, as I have clarified within my report, it is incumbent on a commander to intervene if he is aware, or he or she is aware of a failure of discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can you command soldiers without discipline?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: No. Soldiers cannot be commanded effectively without being -- without them, either the commander or those commanded, without being within a framework of good order and discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can modern armies operate without discipline?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: No armies can operate effectively without discipline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: For an effective maintenance of this discipline, how closely -- how close must the commander be to the operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- as I've stated, Your Honour, within a command system, there are commanders at all levels. For discipline to work effectively, actions must be monitored at all levels. And it also requires that any failings of discipline are reported up that chain of command without delay. A senior commander cannot be present everywhere to monitor the action of his subordinates so in the first instance he must rely on his subordinates to monitor and to ensure good order and discipline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Following up on Judge Moloto's question, can actions be monitored without reporting up? Can a commander learn about disciplinary issues from other sources?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: A commander should use all available sources in order to monitor the situation, but as previously stated, and in fact in one of my answers to His Honour the Judge, I've stated that it's important that regular reports, reports and returns, are maintained up a chain of command. So that is information coming up from below. But in my view, and in my experience, a commander has also responsibility to take active steps himself and that is why, whether it's on peacetime training or on operations, any good commander visits his subordinate commanders and units to confirm their state of operational efficiency which includes their state of discipline.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: In paragraph 3.3.4 which is subtitled "Discipline Within a Multinational Context," what is the general point that you make in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: I think this has already been raised in my responses about the national contingent commander. When a sending state deploys forces into a theatre of operations and subordinates its forces under multinational command, the full command, and hence responsibility for disciplinary matters, is retained under the national command chain. To facilitate that, normally a national contingent commander would be appointed and he has, in the first instance, responsibility to ensure that discipline is maintained within the national element of a multinational force.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page, please, in English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Paragraph 3.3.5 -- excuse me, 3.3. -- and 3.3.6 regarding the obligations of the commander of one of the contributing forces in the event he becomes aware that his personnel that have been placed under the operational control of another force are being engaged in criminal conduct by the foreign commander with operational control, you actually have answered this question in a previous response in the last session. If we turn to paragraph 3.3.8, what further options would be available to the troop contributing nation, in particular if there isn't an appointed national commander in theatre responsible for discipline?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Well, as I've stated, even if a national contingent commander is not appointed formally, de facto there will be a senior national officer present. So either way the action should be available to a responsible individual in a theatre of operations. But notwithstanding that, the contributing nation clearly has in its only interests and its own responsibilities with respect to the action of its forces be they under a multinational command. What I've tried to do here in paragraph 3.3.8 is explore some of the theoretical options available to the troop-contributing nation or sending state. In my experience, however, is that these matters are normally conducted in an informal matter either within the theatre of operations or in more serious cases could be again dealt with in military-to-military contacts at national level.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And when you say dealt with by military-to-military contacts, what kind of contacts do you mean?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Well, that could be -- and again, I would stress to the Court here, I'm painting a theoretical picture here. I'm not giving any -- because I could not find any recent historical examples to clarify this point, so I'm painting a theoretical picture. I imagine that those contacts will be on the basis of phone calls, letters, or whatever. The historical example I gave above that was a real example, but was just to indicate there are limitations to the execution of multinational command when a senior national commander has grave concerns as to the planned conduct of operations. There are systems available for that national commander to air his concerns.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Obviously this presupposes a discussion of the plans between the multinational commander and the national commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And that is the nature of multinational operations because of sensitivities. It's my experience on operations myself or observing operations that multinational operations normally include a degree of prior discussion which would not normally be required of national operations. This is, Your Honour, to avoid nations objecting to executed plans after the event. It is much easier and much better for all parties concerned to have that discussion beforehand so any concerns can be raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And are you aware from your professional experience of a situation where in a multinational effort there's no such prior discussion of plans before execution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Other than the most minor tactical activity, I'm not aware. My own personal operational experience, and again visiting operational theatres, any substantive plan within a multinational context would be normally discussed and rehearsed beforehand, and specifically to allow the national contingents to look at those plans and to agree to them beforehand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Following up on one of Judge Moloto's questions -- actually, no, in one of your responses, you said, General: "It is much easier and much better for all parties concerned to have that discussion beforehand so that any concerns can be raised." Of course, would that exclude the possibility of if plans do not go well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do we have a cell phone ringing?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I hear something, Your Honour, but it's not my cell phone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I didn't suggest it's yours, Mr. Saxon. Okay. It's probably ringing deep in the pocket somewhere. That's fine. Carry on, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If, for example, a plan in a multinational context goes awry, does not turn out well, discussions about -- can discussions about any problems also take place military to military?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could, please, turn to page 21 in the English version. The bottom of page 21 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: On page 21 we see question 4: "Based on commonly accepted principles of military doctrine and practice, what evaluation and review is done before a professional soldier is promoted to a higher rank? Are you aware of any military in which promotion of an officer does not take into account a review of allegations of criminal activity by that officer?" If we can focus, General Melvin, please, on paragraphs 3.4.3 and 3.4.4, page 21, both versions. Those paragraphs deal with the first part of question 4. What kind of evaluation and review is done before a professional soldier is promoted to a higher rank, at least in modern armies that you are aware of?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
