utterances.text: In my experience across the military forces I've either worked with or am aware of or have researched, it is common to say that promotion is based on evaluation of two fundamental matters. Firstly, the performance of the individual, and secondly, his or her potential at a higher rank, and with that, greater degrees of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And what about the selection of officers to very high-ranking posts?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: This varies across armed forces according to their national traditions and systems. Clearly, I'm most familiar with my own armed forces and the British army. All I can say is promotion to the highest ranks is taken in a deliberate manner to ensure that the right quality comes to the top. And I think it's only fair to say that an army or an armed force can only be led if it has individuals of high quality at the top, and therefore, it is in the interests of the armed force to ensure that the promotion system is based on meritorious principles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could turn, please, to page 22 of the English and page 23 of the B/C/S version. Paragraphs 3.4.5 and 3.4.6 of your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Melvin, are you aware of any military in which the process of promotion of an officer does not take into account a review of any allegations of criminal activity by that officer?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: I'm not a legal expert, but to my experience and to my knowledge, I would find it hard to envisage. And I am certainly not aware of any force that would not take into account any allegation of criminal activity. Whether there is a formal review in place, I cannot be that specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Do we take that response to my question as a yes or a no?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: I think you should take my answer as if to repeat the question -- could you repeat more specifically the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Of course I can. Are you aware of any military in which the process of promotion of an officer does not take into account a review of any allegations of criminal activity by that officer?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: The answer to that is, I repeat, no. But I qualify my answer carefully by saying that I cannot state here that in all cases there would be a formal review. All I'm saying here is I'm not aware of any military force would not take into account any allegations of criminal activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If you can turn your mind, please, to paragraph 3.4.7. In your experience, General Melvin, what happens if there are allegations of serious offences against an officer who has been recommended for promotion?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: In my experience, if an individual has been recommended for promotion and subsequent to that recommendation there are allegations of a serious offence, then that promotion would normally be stayed, i.e., put on hold, until those allegations are investigated and the individual is cleared.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, General Melvin, what is the rationale for holding the promotion process in abeyance?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: I think that should be self-evident. No military force would wish, in terms of its efficiency, effectiveness or standing, to promote, unwittingly, individuals who would subsequently be found to have committed serious criminal offences.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could turn, please, to page 23 in the English version and page 24 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, these are your conclusions, and if you could simply focus on paragraph 4.3 briefly, please. In summary, what does any system of command need to function effectively?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: I go back to an earlier part of my report where I talk about command involving decision-making, a leadership, and control. In this conclusion, I wanted to highlight the importance of that control function. That control function rests on commanders and staffs monitoring the situation and, where necessary, actively taking part or taking active steps to get further information and to give direction and guidance to their force. The command system cannot function without this responsive feedback system.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: You mention that the control aspect of command requires effective communications. Why are -- why is a system of good communications important for command?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Because without good communications neither the commander or the commanded will be aware of what is going on. It's important that communications work both ways. I think that's clear. Forces cannot be coordinated and directed or monitored without good communications. Likewise, any subordinate units or formations will not be able to act purposefully if they do not receive the appropriate direction and guidance. And within the overall context, discipline cannot be maintained across the force if that normal communications involving reports and returns are not maintained.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, General Melvin. I would like to review with you a few of the authorities or source materials that you relied upon in the drafting of your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we can turn back, please, to paragraph 2.2, which is on page 5 of the English version and page 4 of the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, I know this is something very dear to your heart and mind. What -- generally, why is the application of terminology important when discussing issues related to command?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Command is one aspect of a doctrine and its practical application. Doctrine, so that it's widely understood and practiced, requires clear definition. And that is why all armed forces, to my knowledge, and certainly the ones that I deal with closely within the alliance, rely on a common understanding based on a common doctrine which in turn is based on a common language. And that's why I've referred here in my report to both NATO and national doctrine and specifically to the NATO glossary of terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn, please, to 65 ter 9588, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we do that, what do you want to do with 9572?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm grateful, Your Honour. In consultation with my colleague, if that could be marked for identification at this time, pending arguments about this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 65 ter 9572 is marked for identification, may it please be given an exhibit number and marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document becomes Exhibit P2772 marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I ask a question to you, sir, here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Don't be guaranteed -- you are not guaranteed an answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, but purely procedural terms. Do I understand what is going on now is the supporting material being annotated as documents to my report, or my report being annotated? I would like that to be clarified for my own understanding so I can answer subsequent questions effectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure I understand what you mean by annotated? You said annotated as what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My question here, Your Honour, is I'm trying to understand what is being talked about at the moment. I've produced a report and various, I think the prosecuting counsel is referring to documents I've used as source material. Is that source material now being used as part of the documentary evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see what you say. Not at this stage yet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Essentially yes, you are right, although I do need to review this material with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you confirm that I'm right?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please see 65 ter 9588, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And General Melvin, this is the document that you refer to in footnote 8 of your report. And we see on the first page it says "Allied Joint Doctrine" then below that "AJP-01(C)." First of all, just briefly, can you tell us what this publication is in general terms?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: This publication represents the highest level allied joint doctrine produced by the alliance, and it's specifically designed to cover the operational level of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, General Melvin, when you use the term the "alliance" you are referring to the NATO alliance; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: That is correct, as indicated on the top of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn, please, to section 0502, which is on page 3 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, you see section 502 is subtitled "Command and Control Terminology." Can you tell us, please, what is significant about this section for the purposes of your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: It confirms the statements I've already made, although the terms "command" and "control" are closely related, they are not synonymous. I've demonstrated that, I think, in my earlier responses. It's important to differentiate between the terms command and control, and that's why I have quoted this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would seek to -- I would ask that 65 ter 9588 be marked for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is so marked. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document becomes Exhibit P2773 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Could we please see 65 ter 9587.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And, General, this will be the document that you referred to in footnote 9 of your report. General Melvin, this document is titled "Army Doctrine Publication Land Operations." Can you tell us who published this?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: This document was published by the British army's General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Did you right this document?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: I wrote parts of it, and I was the editor responsible for its design and final publication.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn, please, to section 609 which starts on page 5 in the English version, page 8 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: We see a subheading called "Decision-Making, Leadership and Control." If you could focus your attention, please, to section, for now, just section 609.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And if we could, please, in the English version move to the next page, please, page 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And at the top of page 6 in the English version in that same section we see the world "control" in bold letters. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Why did you select this section and sections I believe 607, 611 as source material for your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: I did so because I wanted to elaborate on the nature of command and demonstrate the interrelationship between the functions or constituent elements of that have command: decision-making, leadership and control. And it was natural for me to refer back to doctrinal material with which I was very familiar because I had written an earlier version of this in "ADP Volume 2 Command" in 1984, published in 1985, and I returned to that material ten years later, edited it, and produced a new condensed version which you see here in chapter 6 of "ADP Land Operations."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So you author this Chapter 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I authored the chapter 6 of "ADP Land Operations" in entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Just for interest sake, who authored the previous document, the NATO document that you referred to at footnote 8 of your report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would be difficult to find one author, Your Honour. The NATO doctrine writing process depends on a system of a nation being appointed custodian - and that's the NATO term used, custodian - of a document. As far as I can recall, the custodian for allied joint operations is the United Kingdom, and the responsibility for that now rests with a department of our joint structures. But it's written very much more in a collective basis, and I cannot give you the name of the individuals concerned in that writing. I don't know, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Given that the custodian nation was Great Britain, is it -- is there by any chance that you may have contributed to its authoring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the past, and I'm talking about in the period 2002 to 2004, I certainly commented on drafts of this doctrine. And I think it's fair to say that part of the allied joint doctrine does bear a very close resemblance to what I've written, particularly in its description of mission command. But I've not written the NATO doctrine, I've commended on drafts, and I believe, and have good reason to believe that those who have written the NATO doctrine have read what I and my colleagues have written on a national basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Melvin, in section 609 that word "control" is bolded. Is control a passive process, exercise of control?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: No, very much is an active process. It requires not just a matter of receiving reports and returns, active measures have to be taken. And as I've previously stated, a commander and his staff have got to take active steps to make sure they keep abreast of the operational situation. Staff officers will often, on behalf of a commander, inquire of subordinate units and formations as to their operational posture and as senior commanders whether on training or on operations are required, in order to exercise their duty, to visit and keep abreast of the activities of their subordinate formations. So control is very much an active matter and not a passive one.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would ask that 65 ter 9587 be marked for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is so marked. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document becomes Exhibit P2774 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Saxon, would that be a convenient point?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If it's convenient for you, Your Honour, yes, it would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Sorry, we are going to have to take an early break because of other commitments, and we'll come back. I guess we'll, for safety sake, the break was supposed to come at quarter past, we'll come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please show the witness what is 65 ter 9586.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Melvin, this will be the document that you refer to at footnote 11 of your report, page 7. Can you tell us, General, what this document is, please?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: "Army Doctrine Publication, Volume 2, Command" was the second in a series of new army doctrine publications written in the early to mid-1990s. "Command," as the number indicates, was the second of these volumes, the first being "Operations." And I was the principal author of this publication, which I wrote in 1994 and it was published in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we please go to page 3 in the English version, page 3 in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Melvin, we see a subtitle here "The Role of the Commander," and then below that we see another subheading "Creating the Command Climate." Can you tell us, please, what is the command climate and why is it important?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: In civilian terms, the command climate could be loosely ascribed as the working environment. It's the environment in which a commander and staff within a headquarters operate, and more generally across a force it indicates the environment or atmosphere between various levels of command and between various commanders. That's what is meant by the command climate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And why is this concept important?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: The command climate is important because at the end of the day command has to be exercised through individuals. The command climate or working environment reflects an understanding that personal relationships, behaviour, command style, personality are all very important. This is valid, I believe, in all walks of life, but it's especially so under the stress and strain of military conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this exhibit please be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is so marked. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document becomes Exhibit P2775 marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: If we could show, please, 65 ter 9592.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, this is the document that you refer to at notes 18 to 21 of your report. General, can you explain what this document is, please?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: This document, as its title clearly indicates, is the NATO glossary of terms and definitions. It's importance is, as I've indicated earlier, in that it spells out, as a lexicon, definitions of important military terms that are acquired in order to affect a common understanding across the alliance, and as the two primary noted languages are English and French, the glossary is so laid out in this manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn, please, to page 3 in the English version and page 3 in the B/C/S version. And if we could focus on the bottom half of the page in the English version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General Melvin, in the right-hand column in the lower half of the page we see the phrase "full command." Did you use this in your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and I laid that out in the section titled "Full Command," which we've referred to earlier on page 13.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And are there other definitions contained in this NATO document that you used as well in your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I drew and quoted not only the definition of full command, but I quoted the definitions of operational command and operational control, also on page 13 of my report. And also from the very same glossary, I dealt -- I quoted "tactical command" and "tactical control" which are reflected on page 14 of my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And just so the record is clear, General Melvin, what is the difference between operational control and tactical control?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: The difference between operational control and tactical control is, as the definition and the key word of the definition of tactical control, it really relates to local direction movement, et cetera. It has less power authority than operational control. Tactical control really only gives the Superior Commander the authority to coordinate and marshal forces, typically it's used for movement. It can be used, as the name suggests, in a more wider tactical or manoeuvre sense. But it is a lesser command state than operational control.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And perhaps, actually, my question should be more precise. The terms "operational" and "tactical," can you describe the difference then between the two?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: I'll have to provide a slightly extended answer to this question because it is important to understand that the terms operational and tactical here are used in a slightly different way than the terms operational and tactical are used when being ascribed as to a level of war. Let me try and explain what I mean by levels of war, because I did not spell those out in my report. Certainly within NATO doctrine and UK national doctrine we differentiate between three levels of war: tactical, operational and strategic. Tactical control and tactical command do relate to the tactical level more or less. The difficulty is, and this is just a difficulty of both doctrine and practice, operational command and operational control are not specific to the operational level, although on first reading you might assume them to be. Operational command and operational control are used rightly and frequently at the tactical level. This is just a problem of the NATO language and the English language that operational is used for several -- has several meanings. I hope that answers your question satisfactorily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It doesn't to me, Major-General, I'm sorry. When you say tactical control is used at tactical level, it's almost saying to me that technical means technical, and I don't understand. What I'm saying is if you are defining a word and in your definition you use the very word, then I don't get it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, perhaps you misheard me. I deliberately used the word tactical. I did not use the word technical, that has another meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Tactical. I'm talking tactical too. If I said technical, I am sorry, I meant to say tactical.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But what I am saying is -- let me give you an example. You say at page 59, line 15: "Tactical control and tactical command do relate to the tactical level more or less."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. Because the -- but with respect, Your Honour, let me try to elaborate on this because this is very complicated business and it's difficult even for those who are using the terms regularly. The difficulties -- we've got the term tactical being used in slightly different senses, and certainly that is the case in operational. Operational is being used -- can be used in the military in at least two ways. It can define a level of war, such as the operational level of war, or, as is here the case, it can be used more widely. The -- in terms of operational command or operational control. I reiterate, and I use my words very carefully here, the terms operational command and operational control are not restricted to either the operational or the tactical level. It is quite correct within the military terminology to apply the term operational command or operational control solely at the tactical level. Do you wish me to elaborate further, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You don't have to. That doesn't mean I understand you. Probably I'm slow on the uptake. My problem is the question to you was, What is the distinction between the words tactical and operational? And you explain, as I understand you, tactical as applying at the tactical level.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And for me whether it's the first tactical or the second tactical which is in the level, I still don't understand what the difference is between the word tactical and operational as used in this context.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The -- the difficulty, Your Honour, is that the word operational command -- I correct myself, the command state, operational command and operational control are not confined to the operational level of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, but what are they? And I understand what they are not confined to, but what is operational command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The operational command as a command state is that which I've defined and quoted word for word on page 13. That's what operational command is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would it help, Your Honour, if I clarified to the Court the distinction between the tactical, operational, and strategic levels? I'm prepared to do that, though it's not contained in my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know. Now, if you are going to strategy, you are probably going to confuse us even more. Let me just say for my purposes it's fine. Let me hand you back to Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, perhaps I could assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Very briefly, General Melvin, you used the phrase tactical level. Very briefly, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: The tactical level is that level of war where actions are planned and conducted at the lowest levels, the actions in the land environment of anything from a platoon maybe up to a battalion or even brigade level. But that will depend on the context of that particular operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you. And the term operational level that you refer to, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: The operational level is an intermediate level between the tactical and strategic that refers to the higher level planning and conduct of campaigns and major operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Your Honour, I would ask that 65 ter 9592 be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is so marked. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document becomes Exhibit P2776 marked for identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we, please, show the witness 65 ter 9593.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: General, this will be the document that you referred to at footnote 22 of your report. What is this document, General Melvin, please?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: This is the "United Kingdom Ministry of Defence's Manual of Military Law," which is a document that goes back a great deal and has been amended continuously. And what I've quoted here is the most up-to-date version.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we turn, please, to page 5 in the English version and page 3 in the B/C/S version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: And we see section 69 there, and what was it or what is it in section 69 that is significant for your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: What I wanted to do here was to demonstrate that the notion of good order and military discipline had legal force, that it was codified in an act and provides part of the foundation of a military law and military discipline, and one that is quoted regularly to remind individuals that a good order and military discipline is an essential part of an effective and efficient military force. So it's just an example because the terminology within it was close to some of the terminology particularly in terms of discipline which you posed in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this exhibit be marked for identification, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is so marked. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. This document becomes Exhibit P2777. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Before I hand you over to the Defence, Major-General, just one little question: In your experience, does -- has it ever happened that withholding of salaries or promotions or pensions being used in armies as a means of command and control -- as a means of implementing command and control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, to my knowledge, not directly. However, they, as we've discussed earlier, the sanction, particularly in the -- to the effect that a promotion would be stayed when a serious offence has been committed or is alleged to have been committed, I think, does have some force within the disciplinary system of an armed force. What it does ensure is that notwithstanding an individual being selected for promotion, it doesn't give him or her any freedoms. He or her remains -- he or she remains subject to continuing good, ordinary military discipline, good behaviour, and good military efficiency. So only as far as I understand your question, Your Honour, I see it as an indirect role.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah. The reason I ask is precisely because of this very last exhibit that we have seen which prescribes a term of imprisonment as a sanction for breach of any law, and I don't see any reference to withholding of the benefits that I've talked about. And, in fact, I would imagine that it is very seldom that an officer would be up for discipline at the same time as he is up for promotion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So at the time of disciplining, you are not entertaining promotion at that stage, you are entertaining the crime that he has committed and you want to discipline him for that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I fully agree, Your Honour. I fully agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And does it ever happen that then the court marshal would then say, Because of her behaviour that is reprehensible and which is illegal, you are not going to be promoted in the future. Or is that an issue that gets considered when promotion comes and not at the time of discipline?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think in all cases the disciplinary issue would always take precedence. I think the issue of any -- as I've said, any question of promotion would be stayed during any investigation. And I think it is fair to say, Your Honour, as I think you yourself have indicated that the disciplinary process would take its path and, therefore, the question of promotion would not apply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But let me try to put my question one more time. My question really is: Has it ever happened that, as a form of punishment at the time of disciplining, an officer is told that in fact your right to promotion is now being withdrawn, so don't even hope for a promotion in the next couple of months or so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's certainly within the British military system, a sanction, one of the sanctions that could be applied to an individual is a loss of seniority and the individual could be held to marked time and his promotion could be delayed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you show it to us in this exhibit that has just been admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I dont' -- Your Honour, I do not believe that issue is raised or detailed in the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But that exhibit deals with punishment for wrong-doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed. But it's only one of many examples of punishment for wrong-doing. It doesn't, with respect, specify the full legal process which I've indicated which could include a sanction, disciplinary sanction, being taken which has the effect, as you've indicated, of delaying or nullifying a promotion. That can happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That can happen. Has it happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, to my knowledge, disciplinary or administrative action can happen, has happened, where individual's promotion has been either delayed or stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do I understand you, sir, to be may saying that the court marshals in Britain dispense punishment that is not prescribed in the law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not at all. Those -- any punishments imposed in a court marshal is fully within the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have only --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But the punishments seem to be qualified in that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I'm asking if there is any qualification of that kind of punishment in that manual.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not an expert on the manual of military law. What I wanted to do here, as I said, was to give an example. I would need to research that issue further to give you a comprehensive answer. I cannot give you in this court a full exposition of the British legal process and the sanctions imposed. All I can tell you is to my certain knowledge that the sanctions taken are legal and those sanctions can include a postponement or delay in -- have the effect of postponing or cancelling promotion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you have no authority for that proposition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no authority insofar as I have not quoted that authority in my report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Fair enough. And you can't think of one as you sit there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I know because I'm -- one of the areas in which I deal with is -- have dealt with and we -- we distinguish in the British military between disciplinary action and administrative action, and it can be where an individual who may not have gone to -- the weight of evidence may not be sufficient for a court marshal can be held under administrative action and one of the sanctions which can be applied under administrative action is a reprimand or a severe reprimand which will have the effect of delaying an individual's promotion. That reprimand or severe reprimand is also a sanction that could be awarded by a court marshal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it possible for you, sir, to research this further and submit to the Court your authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will have to take further advice on that, but if so directed I will endeavour to do my best to supply supplementary information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are so directed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Often times, when dealing with matters of military, one hears the phrase "a fog of war," which I believe is something that a gentleman by the name of Clausewitz discussed rather extensively with regard to military command and military behaviour. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Yes, sir. A fog of war is quoted and described by Carl van Clausewitz in his work "On War."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the issue of fog of war, obviously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: I'm very sorry to interrupt, but what I think is happening is that General Melvin is trying to take note of the Trial Chamber's directive, and I'm wondering whether he might have a moment to do that before the questions continue. So he doesn't get mixed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Absolutely. If that's what's going on, I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought he was writing "fog of war." Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I thought he was too. I thought he was writing down what I was asking him, but I'll wait to see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could I be provided one minute to complete my note on your direction. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think I've made sufficient note on your direction and am available to answer the counsel's question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Major-General. Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I take it that you were mindful of the question that I asked you while you were writing and don't need to elaborate any further with regard to that question; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: I hope I've answered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excellent. With regard to the underlying issues contained within that description, the fog of war, one of the matters that I believe not only Clausewitz but since certainly that time military theoreticians and practitioners have been concerned about is the clarity of language with regard to orders in the first instance; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I've already elaborated on that, the need for a common understanding and the need for a common military lexicon as evidenced by the requirement for a NATO or national glossary of definitions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Independent of the issue of NATO glossary of definitions, it's something which is of consistent importance within the military; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good. Now, with regard to the need for this clarity of language and specificity of understanding, in large measure, the need for such clarity is so that there aren't mistakes being made at any level within the military command either during peace or during war, to the extent that that could be achieved; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the report that you've drafted and the analysis that you underwent in considering the questions asked as well as your testimony here today, I take it you've paid similar attention to detail and clarity of definition of words and concepts; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: I hope that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: One of the questions that was asked of you by Mr. Saxon was with regard to section 1.5 in which you were asked what input on factual matters you had received from others, and your response was that you had received some input with regard to legal phraseology; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, am I to understand that a factual matter here is a matter of legal phraseology, that you were using those terms interchangeably? Just so I'm clear about the terminology used. Legal phraseology would be definition a concept perhaps, not a fact, which is -- I'm trying to understand just for the moment?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: I'm not following, counsel, your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me put it to you in other terms. Which -- which factual matters with regards specifically to legal phraseology did you receive from others?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: I will need to refer to my report in an attempt to give you an answer on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. If you could do so, please.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Yes, I'm in a position now to give you a specific example where I received advice from a member of the Ministry of Defence's legal services.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excellent. Where would that be, sir?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: That is on page 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. What legal advice --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: And I was advised, and this was inserted at the request of one of the legal officers that I should stress, and I quoted the advice, it is the boxed important note near the top of the -- my report page 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you a little bit, Major-General. Could you sit slightly back away from the microphone. Apparently there are some other noises that get through to the interpreters or somebody else in here. Yeah, that's fine. I think that's a reasonable distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You also might be able to reduce the volume. That might be of some help as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You were -- I take it you were suggesting that where it says a box important note that is the legal phraseology that you were eluding to as being a factual matter that you received from someone else; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: I was stating that this was advice I had been given by a legal officer, and he advised me to include that note.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My question is, that is what you were referring to with regard to section 1.5, which is "I can confirm that I received some input on factual matters from others," so that is the legal phraseology that you are referring to, since that's how you termed it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Indeed. That is one example that I can immediately draw the Court's attention to where I received advice from others.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, just to be clear - because what we are trying to do is be quite specific with our language - advice may be factual or otherwise, so you're use now of the term "advice" as it relates to factual matters. My question to you now, sir, is: Are you equating advice with factual matters? Just so I'm clear about the terminology that you are using, General.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: I'm equating advice and input. My use in paragraph 1.5 some input I could have alternatively used the word some advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to either of those terms, either advice or input, the important note that you've given us as an example that it must be stressed that individual members of a national contingent at all times remain subject to the military law of their own troop contributing nation and to international law is the fact that you are referring to; correct? That's a factual matter in your estimation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: I think you are trying to, with respect, trying to trip me up here. What I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, I'm not trying to trip you up at all, sir. I'm trying to understand the language that you've used.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: I'm -- I'm being very careful here to reiterate that this terminology, this phraseology on page 19 is an example of the advice I was given.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You see, when you look at 1.5, sir, you're saying that the advice you were given was on factual matters. And the question that's being put to you is, Is the statement in the box a fact or not a fact? Is it a factual matter or is it a legal postulation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think I'm qualified to differentiate so precisely between a legal postulation and a fact. All I can say is I took that advice in good faith. I cannot neither confirm nor deny whether you -- whether it is a fact or otherwise. I took it as a piece of advice. I used that example to assist the Court in good faith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just so we are very clear, no one is doubting your good faith, sir. It is merely an attempt to understand what the language is that you have he a used in your report to make sure it's of benefit and assistance to the Chamber. Nothing more than that. So I want you to rest assured that I believe and I'm sure that all of us here do believe that the report written is a report that's written in good faith.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Well, I'm also trying to establish and try to help the Court understand that what I meant here - and, of course, in reflection one can always review one's words - is that I was responsible for the final wording of the report and the analysis contained in that report. I drew advice. I may have given you a bad example of that advice, but I was also advised, for example, to include some NATO definitions. Those NATO definitions are that -- they are definitions, and I've extracted them. I think that is a factual matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. Now, there's been a term which has been bandied about in our conversation, certainly not our conversation but the conversation you've had today, and that is the term "modern army." And I'd like you, if you could, to please define what a modern army is for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: First of all, I think I would just need to refer to one of the questions, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, I'm not asking you to refer to a question, I'm asking you to refer to a definition of a modern army. Excuse me. And if you could define for us what modern army is because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it seems entirely appropriate that if the witness needs to refer to a portion of his report to answer a question, that he be allowed to do so. He certainly was allowed to do that on direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Submitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm now ready to answer the question as put.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I attend to your answer.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: I -- well, first of all I'd like to draw the Court's -- to draw the attention that I don't believe in my report I've used the term "modern army." I referred to modern nation states. What I tried to do here in my report was to distinguish between the historic example and today's contemporary example. Modern army, I don't think can be easily defined in a few words. I will attempt to do so to assist the Court. It's not defined doctrinally anyway, but I will attempt to give you a concise answer. A modern army is a army that uses modern, current, up-to-date equipment, doctrine, training methods, takes into account recent lessons from operations, keeps itself up to date, and addresses the challenges of today. I.e., it is an army fit for today's conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: How would you distinguish, for example, the army fighting in Afghanistan or in Mozambique as opposed to the - let's say an army you are familiar with - the Army of the United Kingdom? Are all three of those modern armies - using your definition - those are armies that -- my question is: Do all of those armies fit within the definition that you have given us, or is there some distinct as between the three of them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: The question refers to the army fighting in Afghanistan. Which army is Mr. Gregor Guy-Smith referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Gregor Guy-Smith is referring to what is called commonly the Taliban.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm happy to answer that question. The notion of modern army does not imply any similarity in terms of approach. It can be an organisation such as the Taliban can use, in my knowledge and experience, certain modern equipments, modern technologies. We are in a difficult area here because we are talking about a state of modernity and also talking about the symmetry of armed forces. One army's modernity can be counter-matched by quite different type of forces' modernity as well. I can elaborate further, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, let me see if I understand what you are saying then and then if I don't, I will be more than happy to have the elaboration. The basic premise of a modern army as I understand what you've just told us is it is an army fit for today's conditions? Is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And would you agree with me that one of the challenges in today's military response is that there are a variety of symmetrical and, if I could, asymmetrical approaches to war that are quite distinct from that which we saw up to perhaps the Korean war? And once again, here is a place where I'm not a historian of war and I, of course, I bow to your expertise.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Well, I think, counsel, you've picked up what I was trying to establish, that one force's modernity can be matched in a different manner. And as you say quite correctly, and reflected my terminology, the forces don't have to be symmetric. And what we are saying today in contemporary conflict, and largely that which we see in Afghanistan, is an asymmetric conflict where the strengths of the western modern warfare are being counter-matched by techniques such improvised explosive devices which are being used in asymmetric manner by the Taliban. However, it is a common misunderstanding, with respect, to believe this is entirely a modern phenomenon. Asymmetric warfare is as old as the Roman Empire. The Second World War, for example, experienced asymmetric warfare, bipartisan, and resistant movements. So warfare has always had a blend of symmetric and asymmetric approaches. The emphasis is that which has changed the character of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what has changed the character of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The character of war, Your Honour, is largely defined by the balance between symmetric and asymmetric approaches. The character of modern war, what we are experiencing today in Afghanistan, is largely defined by the crass distinction between a western force and its asymmetric opponents. Of the Second World War, though it did include asymmetric approaches as I've indicated by partisan and resistance forces, the main character of that war was characterised by the conventional and symmetric approaches of both army, navy, and air forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With that as a working definition of a modern army, we will move on. Now, in your report as well as in your testimony, you have indicated your approach is a detailed and obviously an accurate approach. And I would like to take a moment here with regard to the language that I find on page 13 of your report, and specifically when you were speaking about operational command, or op com. Okay? When you were testifying earlier with regard to this, you quoted on the definition of op com. I just want to make sure once again we are very clear about the language that we are using. You said, this is page 18, line 14, with regard to the question asked by Mr. Saxon, operational command, your answer is: "When we move out of the national realm into the multinational realm certainly within NATO coordination operations involving NATO forces, the most frequent command states used are those of operational command and operational control. Taking the operational command first, to answer your question, is, I quote:" And I take it by that what you mean is that this will be a verbatim recitation of the definition. "... I quote: 'The authority granted to a commander to assign missions or tasks subordinate commanders" -- and then there's a word that's missing here, it says "talks retain or delegate operational or tactical control as the commander deems necessary." Then it says -- and there's an end quote. Now, is that a full verbatim quote of what you are referring to when you guided us to the definition of op com in the operational command definitions which I believe now has been marked as -- excuse me, I'll get it for you. MFI'd as -- I believe it's MFI'd 2775. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I cannot answer that question because I don't have in my memory the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm referring to -- I'm referring to, I'm referring to the NATO glossary of terms and definitions. And it's 2776. So it wouldn't have been of any help to you in any event. But it's the NATO term glossary.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Yes, the glossary. Well, I think I can now assist you. I can confirm to the Court that what I stated on the subparagraph (b) on page 13 is a verbatim quote from the NATO glossary, AAP6, 2009 on page 203, which I referred to at footnote 20 in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, here, and I really don't mean to punch a horse at all, but you go on to say: "I further quote this is the important distinction between operational command and full command, it doesn't include responsibility for administration or discipline." And as I read the definition from whence you read, it doesn't make any mention of discipline in the quote, now, does it?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: No, it doesn't mention -- neither does the definition on full command, but, as I think we've tried to previously establish, that discipline comes under the term administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of quoting, because once again I started my conversation with you in terms of detailed accurate clarifying information, and the importance of the word being used precisely. When I look at this definition, it does say "note" it does not include responsibility for administration. And had you stopped there, sir, I would not be asking you the question that I'm asking you right now. But the definition that you've given us, including those extra words, is not the definition that we have here, is it? And go back and you can look at your glossary.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: I've done that, and I can clarify that the word "or discipline" does not appear either on page 13 of my report, nor does it appear in the glossary.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand that. But it did appear in your testimony, sir, and that's what I'm referring to. "And I further quote ..." that's what the transcript says. "I further quote." And that's what I'm asking you about.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: If I used ill-advisedly the term "I further quote" with relation to discipline, then I apologise to the Court for so doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: But I wanted to make it very clear the distinction on administration, and the Court had already asked me questions as to whether discipline was included under administration. So I was only trying to assist the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. Now, one of the words that you have used throughout your testimony is the word "normally." And I take it that normally has some specific significance with regard to the analysis that you have given us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Can we have, at least, an example where that's been used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I'd be more than happy to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At page 18, line 23: "And I further quote: 'This important distinction between operational command and full command, it doesn't include responsibility normally for administration or discipline.'"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Line?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That was line 23. Page 19, line 11: "Q. Would operational control then include the authority and responsibility to discipline or not? "A. Not normally. The disciplinary chain is normally retained through a full command or national command." I can continue, but I believe that if counsel were to go through a word search on the transcript, he would find numerous examples where the witness has used the word normally in his testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My question to you is with regard to the use of the word normally. Does that have some particular significance with regard to the report that you have penned for us here so we can have some understanding of that?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Are you taking issue with my use of the word normally?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, not at all. I'm trying to appreciate what it means. I'm not taking issue with your use of the word normally at all.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Well, I've used the word normally both in my report and in my testimony because, as the Court will have noted, that my report is based both on doctrine and on my understanding borne of experience. And either doctrine nor experience can account for all eventualities. Doctrine, by definition, provides a framework of understanding, and as an experienced doctrine writer, I will often have to caveat what I write and say by using the word normally because one can never exclude the possibility of variation to the standard approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I'm asking a subtler question, and I don't mean to offend whatsoever. But as I understand your report, your report centres around the following realities, which is, an examination and understanding of the British military system and an examination and an understanding of NATO. And it is these two institutions and the considerations, rules, and regulations that have been promulgated by these institutions from whence you have drawn your conclusions as well as given us the information that you've given us; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: That is correct. As I've stated, I've drawn on NATO national doctrine and my experience within the British armed forces and within NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the issue of "normally," what I'm driving at is that you are referring to a condition, that being the British army, which has operated in a particular fashion and under a particular, not only military, but political environment for some considerable period of time; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And NATO is a combination, as I understand it, and I may well be wrong, but it's a combination of nation states that have come together, each of them having operated in a particular fashion, both of a political as well as military environment of some stability, would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And with regard to the issue of your report, so we are clear, and I think you've alerted us to this right at the very beginning, you said at 2.6, limitation on conclusions, and I want to make sure that I read it properly, so you may want to take a look at it to make sure that I don't offend the accuracy of the words written. "I offer only the most general of conclusions noting that I am not qualified to provide within this expert witness report detailed observations let alone conclusions on the specifics of the case against Momcilo Perisic." Is that -- did I read that accurately?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: That is correct, and I stand by what I've written there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand that. So would it be fair to say - and when I ask you this question, I mean absolutely no disrespect whatsoever - but it would be fair to say that the report as written is of a generic nature with regard to the issues of command, control, and the questions that have been posed to you?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. One of the -- one of the terms that you used in your testimony and you used it -- at one point you said you were talking about "his own nation," and I believe you were referring to the question of somebody's own nation when you were dealing with what was incumbent upon the senior national officer who had been sent from country A to country B. First of all before we go any further, do you recall that testimony? By that I'm referring to the language "those of his own nation."

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: I cannot recall the exact context in which I used the term "his own nation."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Let's see if we can work together here just so we understand what the terminology is that you were using. When you were talking about the senior national officer in the first instance, and you used the term "of his own nation," I take it that what you were referring to is that that senior national officer was a national or a citizen of the sending nation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And he was not, for purposes of our understanding, a mercenary which you have defined actually in your report?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And so we are clear with regard to mercenary, a mercenary is a person who is neither a national of a party to the conflict nor a resident of the territory controlled by party to the conflict. That's one of a series of definitions, I'm -- please, take a look. This, I believe, is your footnote 22. No, that's not correct. I don't mean to --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: I think you mean footnote 16, counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: I included this to make it clear that I was referring to the legitimate secondment of individuals from nation A to nation B and not -- and therefore not anything that could be confused with mercenary, and therefore to give substance to that point, I included a reference to the international convention. That's all I did, to clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to your -- with regard to your clarification in that regard, I note that the international convention is a document that I believe was promulgated in 2001; correct?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: That is the -- the quote or the reference I used. That's the one I found. I'm not aware of any other convention.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. However - and please do correct me if I'm wrong - the principle, the underlying principle therein, that of a mercenary is neither a national of a party to the conflict nor a resident of the territory controlled by a party to the conflict, is something which has been consistently understood and recognised for some number of years, and by that I mean eons, not decades?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Counsel, I'm afraid I really can't speculate on that. I think that's a fair point, but I'm not an expert on this issue on mercenaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. But with regard to the issue of those -- with regard to the issue of "his nation," I take it that was an important component part in your analysis of where the individuals from the sending nation owed allegiance to, and by that I mean they were citizens and owed allegiance to that sending nation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Correct. And remember, this was purely put in to give some context to the secondment. Because that was the questioned asked. It was not about mercenaries, it was asked about seconding of individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue, since you continue to, and I think rightfully so, relate the issue of secondment to the question posed, within the context of secondment is a principle and underlying understanding that the individual or individuals seconded are citizens of a particular nation, that being the sending nation?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Got it. Thank you. That's really quite helpful because I was somewhat confused there. Now, you also mentioned that there were some important issues that existed when dealing with multinational armies or, is the word -- is the phrase "task forces" admissible, or is that taking somewhere we don't want to go?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: That's, sir, I think, too specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Then let's just deal with multinational armies with regard to multinational armies --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Can I interrupt.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: More precisely, bearing in mind our discussions on language, you should be talking about multinational forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excellent, thank you. I appreciate the correction. Multinational forces. We both get the chance to write something down. With regard to the issue of multinational forces, one of the things that you pointed out was the importance of not breaking up the unit?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Yes, and I used the specific example under the command state of operational control that does not empower the multinational commander to break up a subordinated unit of another nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. So put in terms -- put in some concrete terms, just for the moment, looking at the example that you'd given us with regard to Jackson and Clark, Clark is the head of NATO, I think he was the --

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: He was the supreme allied command Europe at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: SACEUR?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: SACEUR.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: SACEUR. He would not have been able to have broken up any of the British units, that was not an authority that he would have had?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: That is correct, he did not have that authority. Though I used that term "example" to show the limitations of orders, I cannot recall precisely the command's names pertaining, but as far as I can recall, the national contingents at the time were under the operational control of headquarters Allied Rapid Reaction Corps, that is as far as I can recall. I visited Kosovo 10 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh. With regard to the issue of authority, his authority derived out of, and I think you've explained this to us, agreements that had occurred before he obtained his position, and that was agreements between a number of nation states who were part of NATO?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Yes, because again as far as I recall there would have been appropriate NATO orders giving substance to the deployment and employment of the multinational force which in this case was the Allied Rapid Reaction Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I think one last question, and I think we'll have to end for the evening, which is: With regard to the agreements, and now speaking specifically about the Jackson/Clark situation that you alluded to in your report, each nation, specifically the UK, had prior to entering in into this joint -- sorry, this multinational force mission?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: A multinational force conducting a mission, a multinational mission. But the substantive point, a multinational force.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Multinational force that the chain of command as far as Jackson was concerned ultimately rested within the British military?

utterances.speaker: ROBERT ADAM MUNGO SIMPSON MELVIN
utterances.text: Yes, because Jackson remained under national command. His force was under -- as far as I can recall, under the operational control of SACEUR.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you so much, and I will see you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Major-General, we are not done with you yet. You'll have to come back tomorrow and -- but before I say when, I need to say to you that between now and when you come back tomorrow, you are not allowed to discuss the case with anybody until you are excused from further testifying. The Court stands adjourned to tomorrow afternoon in quarter past 2 in Courtroom III, not Courtroom II. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
